title: The dry bones (Ezekiel 37)
hookLine: a valley of bones rattles, joins, and breathes

cards: Ezekiel was a priest, carried off to Babylon with King Joachin, years before the city fell. He lived among the exiles by a river called the Chobar, a long way from home.
That's where his visions came, and they were strange. Wheels full of eyes. A scroll he was told to eat.
And this one. The hand of the Lord sets him down in the middle of a valley full of bones. Very many, the text says.

teach.h: CAN THESE BONES LIVE? THOU KNOWEST.
teach.b: God walks him round about them, so he sees how many there are. Then a question, in the Douay-Rheims: "Son of man, dost thou think these bones shall live?"
It's a real question, and Ezekiel hands it back: "O Lord God, thou knowest." So God tells him to preach to the bones: ye dry bones, hear the word of the Lord.

teach.h: BONE TO ITS BONE, BUT NO BREATH.
teach.b: As he speaks there's a rattling, and the bones come together, bone to its bone. Sinews come, then flesh, then skin. And they lie there.
Bodies, but no breath. So God tells him to prophesy a second time, to the breath: come from the four winds, and blow upon these slain, that they may live.
Breath comes into them, and they stand up on their feet, an exceeding great army. The chapter turns on one Hebrew word, ruach.
It means breath, and wind, and spirit. Ezekiel uses it all three ways here, sometimes in one sentence, and English has to pick one each time.

teach.h: OUR HOPE IS LOST, THEY SAID.
teach.b: Then God explains: these bones are the whole house of Israel, the exiles saying our bones are dried up, our hope is lost.
The vision promises that a people who thought they were finished would live and go home.

Christians also hear in it the resurrection of the dead and the gift of the Spirit; the Church reads it at the Vigil of Pentecost and in Lent. Either way, the bones don't argue their way back to life.
They're spoken to, and then breathed into.

how: The Catholic Church reads Ezekiel's vision of the dry bones at the Vigil of Pentecost and on a Sunday in Lent, hearing in it the promise of resurrection and the gift of the Holy Spirit.

s: the bones come fully alive the moment Ezekiel first speaks
first they join and get flesh, but there's no breath in them. the breath comes with a second prophecy.
Ezekiel answers God's question with a yes
he answers: O Lord God, thou knowest.
God explains that the bones stand for the exiles who had lost hope
these bones are the whole house of Israel, saying our hope is lost.

games.q: you're Ezekiel. God shows you a valley of very dry bones and asks: can these bones live? what do you say?
games.why: he hands the question back to God. then God tells him to speak to the bones, and they rattle together.

practice: Let one dried-out thing come to mind: a friendship gone quiet, a hope you stopped mentioning, a part of your faith that hasn't moved in a long time.
Don't try to make it live; just ask over it, can this live?, and give Ezekiel's answer, thou knowest, as you breathe. If you pray, pray over it as it is.

wordCard.voice: ruach. Hebrew for breath, wind and spirit: what entered the dry bones in Ezekiel's valley and made them stand up as a living army. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: breath, wind, spirit. Ezekiel 37 uses it all three ways.
